entries.clue: Internal development rebuilt Worthing (8)

indicatorNotes.rebuilt: A rebuilt thing has been taken to pieces and put up again differently, so the letters beside it are not to be used in the order printed.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

annotation.surface: A seaside town on the south coast being knocked about by the developers.
annotation.walkthrough: Worthing is a resort town in West Sussex, which is why it passes so easily as the object of a building programme. The definition is the medical sense — a nail or a hair turning back into the flesh.
annotation.definitionFit: An ingrowth is growth turned inward instead of outward, so it is development happening internally rather than on the surface.

entries.clue: Resting, having seen off the French vitality (4)

indicatorNotes.having seen off: To see someone off is to get rid of them, so the letters named next are driven out of the word in front.

blocks.note: someone lazing is resting, doing nothing much
the French definite article in its feminine form

annotation.surface: Somebody taking it easy once the French visitors have been shown the door.
annotation.walkthrough: Two French words for 'the' are always in play, LE and LA, and only one of them is sitting at the front of a word for idling. The last word is not part of the French phrase it appears to belong to.
annotation.definitionFit: Zing is liveliness — the spark and energy a thing has when it is full of life — which is what vitality names.

entries.clue: Tight and generally exhausted after a lot of time at work (6)

indicatorNotes.exhausted: A thing exhausted has been drained of everything inside it, leaving only what stood at either end.
indicatorNotes.a lot of: A lot of a word is most of it but not all, so the final letter is left behind.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something follows it, so this pair of letters ends up at the foot of the entry rather than the top.

blocks.note: a stint is a spell of duty put in at a job, here short of its final letter
the outer letters of the word, all that survives once the inside is drained

annotation.surface: A worker worn out by a long stretch on the job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Exhausted' describes the adverb in front of it, not the worker, and it is an instruction to empty a word rather than a state of mind. A stint is a fixed spell of duty, which is what time at work amounts to.
annotation.definitionFit: Tight is the everyday British word for a person who will not part with money, and stingy is that same meanness.

entries.clue: Chance to play? Prize initially withheld (7)

indicatorNotes.withheld: Something withheld is kept back and never handed over, so the letter named is missing from the word it belongs to.

blocks.note: winnings are the prize money a gambler or a contestant carries off
the first letter of that longer word is the one kept back

annotation.surface: A competition where the prize is held back before anybody gets a turn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' arrives before the word it acts on, so the instruction lands on something the solver has not read yet. An innings is a batter's turn at the crease in cricket, which is where the phrase 'had a good innings' comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: An innings is the spell in which a batter or a side gets to bat, so it is literally their chance to play.

entries.clue: Travelling Peru, solo, where lots of people go (8)

indicatorNotes.Travelling: Letters described as travelling have left their places, so they will not be found in the order they are printed.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, the country and the lone traveller together

annotation.surface: A backpacker making their way round Peru without any company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go' is the polite British verb for visiting the lavatory, which is what lets the definition pass as tourism. A superloo is the big coin-operated public convenience found at stations and bus terminals.
annotation.definitionFit: A superloo is a large paid-entry public lavatory, and 'go' is the British euphemism for needing one, so the definition is literal.

entries.clue: Hope to stay active? This treatment may help (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The setter defines by pointing rather than by naming: 'this treatment' is whichever one answers the wish in the first half of the clue, so the phrase identifies the answer instead of standing in for it as a synonym would.

indicatorNotes.active: Letters called active will not sit still, so they are to be rearranged rather than read as they stand.

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

annotation.surface: Someone who wants to keep moving in later life being pointed towards a therapy.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the patient's own wish, so the clue barely looks like wordplay at all. Osteopaths work by manipulating bone and muscle rather than by prescribing anything.
annotation.definitionFit: Osteopathy is a hands-on treatment of the joints and muscles, and 'this' points at the very one the clue's first half has just asked for.

entries.clue: Opening of luggage in black and silver may be a problem for traveller (3,3)

indicatorNotes.Opening of: The opening of a word is where it starts, so only the letter at its front is taken.
indicatorNotes.in: Something put in a pair of things lands between them, so this letter goes inside rather than in front.

blocks.note: jet is the deep black of the fossil gemstone, as in jet-black
the first letter of the word and nothing else
the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum

annotation.surface: A black and silver suitcase being unzipped at the carousel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Opening of luggage' reads as a customs search and comes to one letter. The answer belongs to the same airport as the picture, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing.
annotation.definitionFit: Jet lag is the exhaustion and scrambled body clock that follows a long flight across time zones, the classic complaint of the long-haul traveller.

entries.clue: Thus guided in sin, led astray, though without much impact (15)

indicatorNotes.led astray: Letters led astray have been taken off their proper path, so they end up somewhere other than where they were printed.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder — the whole first half of the clue, down to the little word it opens with

annotation.surface: A moral tale about somebody shown the wrong road and steered into wrongdoing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thus' looks like a connective and is the first four letters of the fodder, which is why the count comes up short for most solvers. 'Impact' here is the impression made on other people, not a collision.
annotation.definitionFit: Something undistinguished leaves no mark on anybody — ordinary enough to be forgotten — which is what making little impact means.

entries.clue: Disallow point about equipment for ship (10)

indicatorNotes.about: A thing placed about another wraps round it, so the letters named next are enclosed by what has already been assembled.

blocks.note: to ban something is to disallow it
a tine is the point of a fork or of an antler
a rig is the equipment set up for a job, from oil rig to lighting rig

annotation.surface: An official refusing to let a piece of kit through on a technicality.
annotation.walkthrough: The two outer pieces are joined before anything is put inside them, so the wrapping happens round a word that never appears in the clue. A brigantine is a two-masted sailing vessel, and rig is a sailing word too.
annotation.definitionFit: A brigantine is a two-masted sailing vessel, square-rigged on the foremast and fore-and-aft behind, so 'ship' is the category it sits in.

entries.clue: Dodgy customers? Senses female moving away (4)

indicatorNotes.moving away: What moves away has gone, so the letter named just before it is no longer part of the word.

blocks.note: to feel something is to sense it
F is the standard abbreviation for female, as on any form

annotation.surface: A shady clientele noticing the woman slip quietly out of the room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slippery customer' is the English idiom for a person who cannot be pinned down, and the fish is where the image comes from. The clue never says which end the F leaves from, because there is only one to take.
annotation.definitionFit: Eels are proverbially impossible to keep hold of, and English calls a shifty person a slippery customer, so the definition leans on both the fish and the phrase.

entries.clue: Not entirely weak in farm building, showing signs of effort (6)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: Not entirely a word means all of it bar the end, so the last letter comes off before anything else is done.
indicatorNotes.in: One thing put in another sits inside it, so these letters land in the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the sty is the pig's building on a farm
the word for feeble, with its last letter left off

annotation.surface: A flimsy pig shed standing up better than expected.
annotation.walkthrough: The insertion splits a three-letter word after its first letter, which is how a container this short still manages to hide. The definition is literal: perspiration is the visible result of hard work.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody sweaty is visibly damp from exertion, which is what effort looks like from the outside.

entries.clue: Church repeatedly hosting school group, note, after a cold reception (10)

indicatorNotes.repeatedly: Repeatedly asks for the same short piece a second time, one copy written straight after the other.
indicatorNotes.hosting: A host takes guests indoors, so the pieces named next go within the letters just assembled.
indicatorNotes.after: In a down entry what comes after sits below, so the assembled block drops underneath the two letters named at the end of the clue.

blocks.note: the article taken as a single letter
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
CE is the Church of England, and the clue asks for it twice over
the parent-teacher association, the body of parents and staff that runs events at a British school
N is the standard abbreviation for note

annotation.surface: A frosty welcome for the parents and teachers meeting in the church hall.
annotation.walkthrough: The doubled church is the trick: those two letters have to be written out twice before anything can be put between them. 'Cold reception' reads as one phrase and is two separate jobs.
annotation.definitionFit: A reception is the way something is received — a warm one, a hostile one — and acceptance is a reception that takes the thing in.

entries.clue: Tortoise festival, source of pride in the past (8)

indicatorNotes.source of: The source of a word is where it starts, so its opening letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: a gala is a festival or festive occasion
the first letter of the word, on its own
what happened in the past happened so long ago

annotation.surface: A carnival the town has been proud of for years.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Source of pride' looks like the reason for the festival and is a single letter. The word is Spanish for a tortoise, and the Galapagos Islands were named by Spanish sailors for the giant ones they found there.
annotation.definitionFit: Galapago is the Spanish word for a tortoise, taken into English dictionaries, and it is the word behind the name of the islands famous for them.

entries.clue: Very busy, that man, tense, collared by military boss (6)

indicatorNotes.collared by: To be collared by somebody is to be seized and held, so this letter is caught inside the piece named next.

blocks.note: the pronoun standing in for a man already mentioned
the Commander-in-Chief, the officer at the top of an armed force
T is the grammarian's abbreviation for tense

annotation.surface: A jumpy man being grabbed by the scruff of the neck by his commanding officer.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'tense' invites you to read it as another description of the man, when it is a single letter waiting to be swallowed. CIC is ordinary shorthand in military writing.
annotation.definitionFit: A hectic day is one crammed with rushing from thing to thing, which is what being very busy feels like from the inside.

entries.clue: Island, regarding grass crop, mostly undeveloped (8)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly a word is all of it but the final letter, so the last one is left off.

blocks.note: inch is the Scottish word for a small island, as in Inchcolm and Inchkeith
oaten means of or concerning the oat, a grass grown as a cereal, and its last letter goes

annotation.surface: An island where the cereal harvest has hardly been improved at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inch' for island comes from the Gaelic innis and survives in Scottish place names rather than in dictionaries most solvers reach for. Oats are a grass grown as a crop, so the farming sense is the one wanted and not the slang one.
annotation.definitionFit: Something inchoate has only just begun and has not yet taken shape, which is exactly what undeveloped describes.

entries.clue: What follower may do twice, getting soldier’s ID (3,3)

indicatorNotes.twice: Twice asks for the instruction to be obeyed a second time, so two different words for the same action go side by side.

blocks.note: to dog somebody is to follow them persistently
to tag along is to follow behind, the second answer the instruction asks for

annotation.surface: Somebody trailing another person through the streets, over and over.
annotation.walkthrough: English keeps two verbs for following, and the clue quietly asks for both. Dog tags are the stamped identity discs a soldier wears on a chain round the neck.
annotation.definitionFit: A dog tag is the metal disc a soldier wears so the body can be named, so 'soldier's ID' is what the thing is for.

entries.clue: Good to spike cocktail of gin, decorating with sugar (8)

indicatorNotes.cocktail of: A cocktail is things stirred together, so the letters that follow go into a new order.

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report
to lace a drink is to spike it with spirits
three letters stirred into a different order

annotation.surface: Someone slipping spirits into the punch at a party.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinks vocabulary runs the length of the clue — spike, cocktail, gin — and none of it survives into the answer. Glacé means coated in a sugar glaze, which is where the glacé cherry gets its name.
annotation.definitionFit: To glace something is to give it a glossy sugar coating, so glaceing is the act of decorating with sugar.

entries.clue: Family and God animated millions in country (7)

indicatorNotes.animated: Something animated has been set moving, so those letters will not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: one's kin are one's family
three letters set moving into another order
M is the abbreviation for millions, as in a set of accounts

annotation.surface: A household and its deity brought to life on screen for millions abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: A three-letter shuffle is the easiest anagram to read straight past, and 'animated' is doing it to the word you would least expect to be fodder. The capital letter is the setter's, not a clue to anything.
annotation.definitionFit: A kingdom is a country with a king or a queen at its head, so 'country' is the plain category it belongs to.

entries.clue: Italian navigator against having drinks in reserve, made to backtrack (8)

indicatorNotes.in: Drinks put in the reserve go inside it, so these letters are planted within the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.made to backtrack: To backtrack is to retrace the way you came, so across the grid that part is read from its far end.

blocks.note: v for versus, as printed in any fixture list
something kept on ice is being held in reserve
cups are drinks, as in a cup of tea

annotation.surface: A fixture with the refreshments held back in store and everybody sent back the way they came.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On ice' is the English idiom for keeping something in reserve, and that is the word the drinks go into before the whole lot turns round. Amerigo Vespucci is the Florentine whose voyages gave America its name.
annotation.definitionFit: Amerigo Vespucci sailed to the New World for Spain and Portugal and the continent was named after him, so 'Italian navigator' names the man.

entries.clue: Upset the old, about to leave union in dramatic situation? (6)

indicatorNotes.Upset: Upset means turned over, and in a down entry turning something over means reading it from the bottom up.
indicatorNotes.about: A thing placed about another goes round it, so these letters end up on either side of the word that follows.

blocks.note: ye is the old form of 'the', as in Ye Olde Tea Shoppe
to quit is to leave

annotation.surface: Older members annoyed, and on the point of walking out of a theatrical row.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The old' is not the elderly: it is the archaic spelling of 'the', and it supplies the two letters at either end. The question mark is there because the definition names one union rather than unions in general.
annotation.definitionFit: Equity is the British trade union for actors, stage managers and other performers, so the union found in a dramatic situation is the theatrical one.

entries.clue: Attack West always put down (6)

blocks.note: W is the compass abbreviation for west
ay is the old poetic word for ever, as in 'for ay'
to lay a thing is to put it down

annotation.surface: A westerner who was forever being belittled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put down' is the literal action of setting something on the ground, not the insult the surface offers. To waylay is to lie in wait beside the road and fall on a traveller, so the definition is the highwayman's sense.
annotation.definitionFit: To waylay somebody is to lie in wait and set upon them, which is an attack made by ambush rather than head on.

entries.clue: Footballer’s victory over Germany (6)

indicatorNotes.over: In a down entry one thing over another sits above it, so the first piece goes on top and the country's letters underneath.

blocks.note: a win is a victory
GER is the three-letter country code for Germany used on scoreboards

annotation.surface: A player's win against the Germans.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is football and so is the answer, which is rarer than it sounds: the definition gets to hide by telling the truth. A winger plays wide, out by the touchline.
annotation.definitionFit: A winger is the player stationed on the flank by the touchline, one of the standard positions in a football side.

entries.clue: Reversed objection to a brass instrument (4)

indicatorNotes.Reversed: Reversed means read the other way round, and across the grid that is right to left.

blocks.note: 'but' is the word an objection begins with, turned round
the article taken as a single letter

annotation.surface: Somebody taking back their complaint about a piece of brass.
annotation.walkthrough: The reversal is flagged before the word it acts on has been read, so the instruction lands on nothing at first. 'But' is the objection, not 'no', because only one of them reads as something else backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: The tuba is the big low-voiced member of the brass family, the bottom of the band, so 'brass instrument' is the group it belongs to.

entries.clue: Excitedly sing opera around quiet musical features of church (5,5)

indicatorNotes.Excitedly: Anything done excitedly is not done carefully, so the letters come out in a different order from the printed one.
indicatorNotes.around: One thing around another closes over it, so the shuffled letters open up to take in the letter that follows.

blocks.note: nine letters rearranged, ready to be opened up
p is piano, the musician's mark for quiet

annotation.surface: An enthusiastic performance of opera being sung softly in a church.
annotation.walkthrough: The shuffle is done first and the result is then split open, so the letters you rearrange are not the letters you write down in one run. Every word of the surface is musical, which is what keeps the mechanism out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Organ pipes are the ranks of metal and wooden tubes that sound the organ, and in Britain they are the one piece of musical apparatus almost every church has.

entries.clue: Some budding author’s Scandinavian name (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a phrase is a part of it, and the part wanted here is a run of letters already sitting in the words as written.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters, running off the end of the first word and into the start of the second

annotation.surface: A young writer with a Nordic first name.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden runs cross a word boundary precisely because the eye reads words rather than letters, and here the join is between a participle and a noun. Inga is an everyday given name in Sweden, Norway and Denmark.
annotation.definitionFit: Inga is an ordinary woman's first name right across Scandinavia, so the definition names the family of names it comes from.

entries.clue: Insist on shunning crossbows? (5,2,4,4)

blocks.note: The straight reading: holding to a position and refusing to be argued out of it.
The setter's reading is literal — a shooter who will have nothing to do with bows is left with only the other sort of weapon, and keeps to it.

annotation.surface: A marksman who refuses to have anything to do with crossbows.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom is being taken at its word: turn down the bow and firearms are the only weapons left to keep to. A crossbow shoots bolts rather than bullets, so the two the clue sets against each other really are different things.
annotation.definitionFit: To stick to one's guns is to hold your position under pressure, which is what insisting on something is, and shunning crossbows leaves you keeping literally to guns.
